blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, when things happen, they all happen at once. How true the old sayings are! I shall be twenty in September. Yet until today, no one had ever asked me to marry him—not seriously. And today three men have asked me. Just imagine! THREE offers of marriage in one day! Isn’t it awful! I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I don’t know what to do with myself. And three offers of marriage! But please, please don’t tell any of the girls. They would get all sorts of wild ideas. They would feel hurt and badly treated if they did not get at least six offers on their very first day at home. Some girls admire themselves so much! You and I, Mina dear, are engaged. Soon we shall settle down into the serious lives of old married women. We can look down on girls who think so much of themselves. Well, I must tell you about the three men. But you must keep it a secret, dear, from everyone except, of course, Jonathan. You will tell him. If I were in your place, I would certainly tell Arthur. A woman ought to tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear? And I must be fair. Men like women, certainly their wives, to be just as fair as they are. And I am afraid women are not always quite as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, number One came just before lunch. I told you about him: Dr. John Seward, who works at the hospital for mentally ill people. He has a strong jaw and a fine forehead. He appeared very calm, but he was nervous all the same. Clearly, he had trained himself to remember all sorts of little things, and he remembered them. But he almost sat down on his silk hat. Men don’t usually do that when they are calm. Then he wanted to look relaxed, but he kept playing with a small, sharp medical knife. It almost made me scream. He spoke to me very directly, Mina. He told me how much I meant to him, although he had known me for so short a time. He told me what his life would be like with me to help him and make him happy. He was going to say how unhappy he would be if I did not love him. But when he saw me cry, he said he was a cruel beast. He said he would not make me more upset than I already was. Then he stopped and asked if I could grow to love him. When I shook my head, his hands shook. Then, after a short pause, he asked if I already loved someone else. He asked very kindly. He said he did not want to force me to tell him my secrets. He only wanted to know, because a man could hope if a woman’s heart was free. And then, Mina, I felt that perhaps I ought to tell him there was someone. That was all I told him. Then he stood up, looking very strong and very serious. He took both my hands in his and said he hoped I would be happy. He said that if I ever needed a friend, I must consider him one of my best. Oh, Mina dear, I can’t help crying. You must forgive all the marks my tears have made on this letter. Having someone ask you to marry him is very nice and all that. But it is not at all happy when you have to watch the poor man leave. You know he truly loves you, and he looks as if his heart is broken. And whatever he may say at that moment, you know you are leaving his life completely. My dear, I must stop here for now. I feel so terribly sad, although I am so happy.

“Arthur has just gone, and I feel happier than when I stopped writing. So I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, number Two came after lunch. He is such a nice man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and so fresh. It seems almost impossible that he has visited so many places and had such adventures. I understand how poor Desdemona felt when stories of danger poured into her ear like a stream, even from a black man. I suppose we women are such cowards that we think a man will save us from our fears. So we marry him. Now I know what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I don’t. Mr. Morris told us his stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet—— My dear, I am getting ahead of my story. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems that a man always does find a girl alone. No, he doesn’t. Arthur tried twice to arrange a chance, and I helped him as much as I could. I am not ashamed to say it now. First, I must tell you that Mr. Morris doesn’t always use slang, those informal words people use in conversation. He never uses it when speaking to strangers, or when they are there. He is really well educated and has extremely good manners. But he discovered that I enjoyed hearing his American slang. Whenever I was there, and no one else would be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my dear, he has to invent it all. It fits exactly with whatever else he has to say. But slang does work like this. I don’t know if I shall ever use slang myself. I don’t know whether Arthur likes it, as I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat down beside me and looked as happy and cheerful as he could. But I could still see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his and said very sweetly:—
